title: Binary search
summary: When a yes/no test flips only once across sorted data, check the middle and throw away the half that cannot hold the answer.
idea: Sorted order means one comparison at the middle rules out half the range. Halving n items takes about log₂ n steps.

signals.see: The input is sorted and you must find a value or a position.
signals.think: Keep lo and hi around the part that can still hold it. Compare the middle and drop one half.

signals.see: You need the first or last position where something becomes true.
signals.think: Do not stop at a match. Keep shrinking toward the boundary and return lo at the end.

signals.see: The question asks for O(log n) time.
signals.think: That almost always means halving the search range each step.

signals.see: You must find the smallest or largest setting that still works, like a speed or a capacity.
signals.think: Binary search on the answer itself. See the search-on-the-answer sub-page.

phrasings: Product ids are sorted. Report where id 4182 is, or -1 if it is missing.
Given sorted exam scores, how many students scored at least 70?
A version list is sorted and the build broke at some version. Find the first broken one.

picture.title: Halve the range each step
picture.alt: On the left, every item is checked from the start, costing up to n steps. On the right, the middle of the range is compared with the target and half of the range is dropped each time, so about log n steps are needed.
picture.caption: A million sorted items need about 20 checks.

code.py:
def search(nums, target):
    lo, hi = 0, len(nums) - 1  #@init
    while lo <= hi:  #@loop
        mid = (lo + hi) // 2  #@mid
        if nums[mid] == target: return mid  #@found
        if nums[mid] < target: lo = mid + 1  #@right
        else: hi = mid - 1  #@left
    return -1  #@none

visualiser.inputHelp: Up to 12 different whole numbers between -99 and 99, smallest first, separated by commas. The target is between -99 and 99.

oneLiner: lo, hi = 0, n; while lo < hi: mid too small → lo = mid + 1, else hi = mid; return lo

exercise.prompt: nums is sorted from smallest to largest and may contain repeats. Return the first index whose value is at least target, or nums.length if there is none. That is where target would be inserted. The starter stops as soon as it sees target, which can miss earlier copies. Fix it so it always finds the first one.
hints: A match at mid might not be the first one. Keep mid as a candidate by setting hi = mid instead of returning.
Delete the equality check. With lo < hi and hi = mid, the loop ends with lo at the first value >= target.

complexity.why: Each step halves the range that can hold the answer, so n items need about log₂ n steps. Only lo, hi and mid are stored.

mistakes: Mixing loop styles: with lo <= hi move both bounds past mid; with lo < hi keep hi = mid.
Setting lo = mid with mid rounded down, which loops forever when hi = lo + 1. Round up instead.
Returning on the first match when the question asks for the first or last position.
Running binary search on unsorted data. The yes/no test must flip only once.
Forgetting the not-found case, such as returning lo without checking that nums[lo] equals the target.

quiz.question: With the loop while lo < hi and hi = mid, why must lo move to mid + 1 rather than mid?
choices: Otherwise the range can stop shrinking and loop forever
quiz.explain: mid rounds down, so when hi = lo + 1, mid equals lo. Setting lo = mid would change nothing, forever.

quiz.question: You need the first index of a value that appears many times. What do you do on a match?
choices: Keep mid as a candidate and search the left half
quiz.explain: An earlier copy may exist, so keep shrinking left (hi = mid) until lo and hi meet.

quiz.question: About how many steps does binary search need for 1,000,000 sorted items?
quiz.explain: 2²⁰ is about a million, so halving reaches one item in about 20 steps.

interviewTip: Say what range [lo, hi] means before coding, for example “the answer is always inside it”. Then each update is easy to justify and off-by-one bugs disappear.
